items.title: Shakespeare takes centre stage at Lecce’s Carlo V Castle
items.summary: A journey into the Bard’s world is captivating Salento from the underground chambers of Puglia’s largest fortress, with a possible extension until next spring.
items.content:
There is a place in Lecce where 16th-century walls seem to whisper the secrets of history’s greatest playwright, and where the boundaries between reality, illusion and madness dissolve into the darkness of underground chambers.

This is Carlo V Castle, originally built in the 12th century during the Norman period. Since last July, it has been hosting The Matter of Dreams: Worlds and Visions in Shakespeare’s Works.

The good news is that organisers are considering extending the exhibition until at least next spring. It was originally scheduled to close on January 10.

If, as Shakespeare famously wrote in The Tempest (Act IV, Scene I), “We are such stuff as dreams are made on”, then Lecce’s fortress – the largest castle in Puglia – is the perfect setting for an immersive journey into the Bard’s universe.

“The choice of this venue was by no means accidental,” explains Pietro Copani, director of Carlo V Castle. Lecce’s strong theatrical tradition further strengthens the connection between the exhibition and the city.

Conceived and created by Peter Bottazzi and Silvia Rigon, this original international project is promoted by the Swabian Castle of Bari, part of the Regional Directorate of National Museums of Puglia.

Bringing an undertaking of this scale to life took time. Two years were needed to conceive, develop and design the entire exhibition, bringing its multimedia elements together with the scholarly rigour ensured by Michael Dobson, director of the Shakespeare Institute in Stratford-upon-Avon, who served as an adviser to the project.

The exhibition unfolds through the castle’s atmospheric underground chambers and features seven major multimedia installations.

The journey begins with Prospero’s Ship, inspired by the central character in The Tempest and symbolically made up of all Shakespeare’s works. It is an immersive soundscape featuring poetic verses read in 40 languages.

Next comes the Shakespeare Workshop, an educational and documentary space exploring the playwright’s life and body of works.

Visitors then encounter Soliloquy, an intimate, multisensory environment built around Hamlet’s famous “To be or not to be” speech, inviting reflection on life’s great existential dilemmas.

The Fantastic transforms words into visual experiences through video mapping and songs from The Tempest, Macbeth, A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Hamlet.

The journey continues with Radio Shakespeare, an evocative soundscape exploring the power of listening, voice and theatrical memory, and Through Words, where pages and verses seem to dissolve into light across the castle’s stone walls, tracing the transmission of literary heritage through time.

The final installation, Between the Cracks of Power, revisits the dramatic tensions, conspiracies and betrayals typical of Shakespeare’s history plays.

“Rather than simply telling Shakespeare’s story, we wanted to convey his extraordinary ability to inspire new questions, interpretations and forms of imagination, even today,” explain curators Bottazzi and Rigon.

“The collaboration with the Shakespeare Institute and the interdisciplinary nature of this initiative reflect our commitment to developing projects with an international outlook, bringing places of outstanding historical value into dialogue with new forms of storytelling and public engagement,” says Anita Guarnieri, director of the Swabian Castle of Bari and the Regional Directorate of National Museums of Puglia.

Maria d’Enghien, Countess of Lecce and later Queen of Naples, ruled the city and chose the castle as her permanent residence from 1420 until her death in 1446.

The fortress underwent its most significant transformation between 1537 and 1550, on the orders of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V of Habsburg. To defend against Ottoman invasions, the old medieval structure was incorporated into an Italian-style fortress with imposing angular bastions, designed by military engineer Giangiacomo dell’Acaya.

Over the centuries, the castle has served many purposes: a barracks, a courthouse and a military district, before eventually being returned to the city as a cultural centre.

Hidden beneath the medieval Torre Mozza, the castle’s underground chambers contain one of its most evocative areas: the old prisons. They hold stories of human tragedy and extraordinary twists of fate. Among those who died here in extreme poverty was Giangiacomo dell’Acaya himself, the very architect who had designed and built the fortress.

The royal engineer was imprisoned within the walls he had conceived after falling into financial ruin when he acted as guarantor for a debtor who defaulted on his obligations. Over the years, the cells also held prominent figures from Salento’s intellectual and cultural circles, including the thinker Vittorio Prioli.

A visit to the exhibition is best combined with a guided tour of the fortress, which takes in the historic prisons, covered in graffiti, the Maria d’Enghien Hall and the Papier-mâché Museum.

Housed in the castle’s former stables, the museum is a unique gem showcasing around 80 masterpieces of Salento’s traditional papier-mâché craft, which dates back to the 18th century. Many depict sacred figures once carried through the streets in religious processions.

Carlo V Castle is open Tuesday to Sunday, from 10 am to 8 pm.

Castle guided tour and admission to the on-site museums: €10.

For further information and bookings, visit www.ilcastellodilecce.it .

items.title: Swap goods or skills for a stay: Italy's Barter Week is back
items.summary: Photography, gardening, vintage finds, olive oil and wine: an initiative by Bed-and-Breakfast.it, running from 16 to 22 November, invites travellers to discover a different approach to travel and accommodation
items.content:
A 120-bass accordion, for instance. Or a vintage advertising sign, a few bobbin-lace-making lessons, or even a project to bring bees back to an old garden.

This is not a list of unusual purchases: it is the wish list drawn up by Italian B&B hosts taking part in Barter Week, which runs from 16 to 22 November 2026.

The initiative, launched by Bed-and-Breakfast.it and now in its 18th edition, is based on a simple idea: enjoy a stay without money changing hands, offering something in return that might prove useful or interesting to your host.

You don't necessarily need valuable possessions or extraordinary talents to take part. A skill, a passion, a few hours of work or a product from your home region can all serve as currency.

The possibilities range from photography and gardening to maintenance work, website design, computer lessons and help with managing social media accounts.

Among the most common requests are extra-virgin olive oil, wine, cheese and local food specialities. Some hosts even suggest swapping hospitality itself: a few nights at their own B&B in exchange for a stay at another property, perhaps in a region they have yet to discover.

But it is the initiative's online wish list that really brings out the more unusual side of the project. And there is no shortage of ideas to suit every taste.

Relais Accademia, for example, is looking for a vintage advertising sign, either enamelled or neon. Flower Bed & Breakfast, meanwhile, is offering a stay in exchange for a 120-bass accordion.

Ma Che Idea would love to find someone willing to teach its hosts the traditional art of bobbin lace-making, while La Finestra sul Giardino is on the lookout for an illustrator to create a children's book.

In Puglia, at Masseria Murgia Albanese, bartering can even turn into a small environmental project. The aim is to restore a bee-friendly garden of around 500 square metres surrounding an eighteenth-century apiary, to attract bees again.

Further south, in Salento, Giardino Frannicola is looking for artists willing to help create an open-air gallery, with works inspired by local history and traditions. Elsewhere, the requests include old books and magazines published between 1968 and 1977, or a stone laundry basin that can be restored and repurposed as a decorative feature on a terrace.

Behind these seemingly disparate requests lies a vision of hospitality that goes beyond simply providing a bed for the night.

For B&B hosts, bartering can be a way to meet a practical need, bring a shelved project to life or connect with people who share their interests.

For travellers, it offers the chance to build a relationship with a place and the people who live there, contributing something of their own rather than simply paying for a room. After all, the value of an exchange cannot be measured in money alone.

Taking part is straightforward: visitors to the initiative's website can search for participating B&Bs by destination or browse the Wish List.

Once they have found a property, they simply contact the host directly to suggest an exchange, either by responding to an existing request or putting forward an idea of their own. The length of the stay and the terms of the arrangement are agreed between the two parties.

Although the event officially runs from 16 to 22 November, some participating properties are happy to arrange barter stays throughout the year.

After all, sometimes you don't need a credit card to travel: just something to offer.

items.title: Alessandro Carloni: “I drew inspiration from Roberto Benigni for my ‘Cat in the Hat’”
items.summary: The animated film co-directed by the Italian filmmaker has grossed $20 million in the US, putting it second at the box office behind Godzilla Minus Zero
items.content:
Rome – “In America, the Cat in the Hat is a bit like Pinocchio in Italy,” says Alessandro Carloni, the Bologna-born director who has made his mark in Hollywood with Kung Fu Panda and How to Train Your Dragon. He is talking about Warner Bros.’ animated film, which he co-directed with Erica Rivinoja.

On its opening weekend, the Cat in the Hat found itself chasing a monster at the box office: the film took $20 million in the US, $10 million less than Godzilla Minus Zero. In Italy, where the Japanese film opened on 12 November, The Cat in the Hat has grossed €1 million – not a bad result, considering the character created by Dr Seuss has historically struggled to find success on the big screen.

“I was developing three films for Netflix, one of them with Paul McCartney. Then there was a change in leadership, and 25 projects were cancelled. Meanwhile, Warner Bros. had acquired the rights to the Cat in the Hat and approached Erica Rivinoja and me.”

“In the book, the children are bored, indecisive and frightened at the beginning. By the end, they have become more self-confident. I saw the Cat as a clown, or a kind of psychologist – an emotional support animal.”

“Yes. My mother has Alzheimer’s, and I'm gradually saying goodbye to her. Meanwhile, I've had a little girl of my own and watched my wife become a mother. Becoming a parent changes your identity. I used to be an illustrator, a writer, a director. Now I'm a dad.”

How do you strike the right balance between comedy and tears?

“When I was a child, I watched Back to the Future. At the end, when the photograph of the siblings reappears, I cried. Not even a drama had ever moved me that much. If you can make someone laugh, they're more open to being moved afterwards.”

“When I first met my wife, she had to go to the police headquarters to sort out some paperwork. It was mind-numbingly boring. But I was so in love with her that I thought it was wonderful just to go along. It's the same with a character: if you love them, you want to spend time with them, whatever they're doing.”

“During the first screenings, Po came across as obnoxious, convinced he was amazing. Then we turned him into a lovable softie who adores kung fu, and audiences fell in love with him.”

“He may seem like a bit of a charlatan, but everything he does is out of love. He wants to help the children. And he succeeds.”

“Yes. His characters always seem like children trapped inside grown-ups. I dream of creating a new mythology: whenever a child feels sad, the Cat comes along to cheer them up, just like Father Christmas.”

“My father was an illustrator and worked at Gamma Film in the 1950s. He loved abstraction and taught me to simplify images to make them more emotionally powerful. We've eliminated shadows and reflections. It's made on a computer, but it looks hand-drawn.”

“I love characters who exist in silence, who communicate through their eyes. In American cinema, dialogue is written for the audience; in Italian cinema, there's more spontaneity. I left Italy when I was 17, but that sensibility has stayed with me.”

“The ones featuring the ‘Things’. We had no idea what to do with them at first. Then we came up with a language built around rhythm and melody. For two weeks, I drew storyboards and recorded handclaps. When we showed our work to the studio, everyone burst out laughing.”

“I wrote it into the film as a joke, but I really hope it happens.”

items.title: Ebola in Congo: come tutto è iniziato
items.summary: Ebola in Congo: come tutto è iniziato
items.content:
L'analisi dei dati telefonici e, con essi, degli spostamenti della popolazione della Repubblica Democratica del Congo la scorsa primavera ricostruisce le prime fasi di diffusione sottotraccia del virus Ebola Bundibugyo.
Il ceppo del patogeno che da sei mesi imperversa nel Paese africano, e che ha brevemente interessato anche Kenya e Nigeria, ha causato almeno 10.668 casi confermati, inclusi 5.198 decessi, in 67 zone sanitarie di 8 province. Circa la metà (il 48,7%) delle persone contagiate muore, a riprova della difficoltà nell'individuazione precoce dei casi e nella somministrazione di cure tempestive.. Da tempo si sospettava che il primo caso dell'epidemia di Ebola in corso, denunciato dalle autorità sanitarie il 15 maggio 2026, non fosse che la punta dell'iceberg di un sommerso che sobbolliva da settimane. Un nuovo studio pubblicato su Science ha usato le informazioni sulla mobilità dei cittadini per scavare in quei primi anelli della catena di diffusione e restituire una risposta scoraggiante: se ci fossero state più risorse sanitarie sul territorio, forse la corsa del virus si sarebbe potuta rallentare prima.. I primi sintomi già ad aprile. Secondo gli autori dello studio, 42 ricercatori internazionali guidati da Dav M. Ebengo, dell'Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB) di Kinshasa (Repubblica Democratica del Congo), il primo paziente positivo a Ebola avrebbe iniziato a manifestare sintomi il 25 aprile 2026. Un altro caso sospetto sarebbe stato testato il 9 aprile, ma il test ha dato risultato nullo. . Confrontando i dati anonimizzati dei cellulari con i dati dettagliati sui primi casi, gli scienziati hanno scoperto che gli spostamenti umani contribuirono in modo determinante alla prima espansione di Ebola, in particolare tra il 10 maggio e il 1° giugno, periodo in cui il numero di zone e aree sanitarie che segnalavano casi positivi è aumentato molto rapidamente.. Gli spostamenti delle persone dalle città di Mongbwalu, Bunia e Rwampara (nella provincia di Ituri) tra il 24 aprile e il 24 maggio hanno contribuito a prevedere quali zone sanitarie avrebbero segnalato contagi entro il 1° giugno. Le aree vicine ai focolai iniziali presentavano un rischio maggiore di infezioni, ma anche località distanti 150-200 km dai centri iniziali disseminate su percorsi molto battuti verso città o Paesi più grandi sono stati centri importanti di contagio.. Un ceppo insolito in un territorio depotenziato. La conclusione amara dello studio è che i sistemi di sorveglianza hanno fallito nell'individuare prontamente le avvisaglie di un possibile focolaio di Ebola, per due principali motivi. Il primo riguarda il ceppo, Ebola Bundibugyo, meno conosciuto: un sottotipo di Ebola diverso dal ceppo Zaire che ha causato la maggior parte delle maggiori epidemie di Ebola in Africa.
Se per Ebola Zaire sono ampiamente disponibili test diagnostici (oltre a due tipi di vaccini e terapie a base di anticorpi monoclonali), contro Ebola Bundibugyo non sono ancora disponibili vaccini approvati (ci sono per ora due candidati vaccini), e nella provincia di Ituri non c'erano i test: solo le grandi strutture sanitarie regionali ne avevano. Anche per questo il virus è sfuggito alle prime possibili identificazioni.. Il secondo motivo è il definanziamento dei programmi sanitari di comunità dovuto ai tagli agli aiuti esteri dell'USAID decisi da Trump. Questa penuria di risorse ha influito sulla mancata sorveglianza sul territorio, il primo presidio in cui di solito emergono criticità, sintomi insoliti e casi sospetti..

items.title: Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
items.summary: Rescuers found the pet cat in the ruins of Zariah's apartment four days after she made an emotional plea to the public.
items.content:
A teenage girl and her cat have been reunited four days after a building in the New York borough of Brooklyn collapsed.

Zariah Coleman, 13, made an emotional plea when her pet went missing after she and her family were forced to relocate when the side of their building was stripped off in the unexpected collapse.

City officials later found her cat, Isaac, in the debris of the their home and shared the reunion on Sunday afternoon.

Eight people died and 18 others were injured when the three-storey building collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood last Wednesday.

items.title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo dies age 80
items.summary: Known as the 'Boss of Bosses', he was the head of all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s before his arrest broke up his drug organisation.
items.content:
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.

Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.

Known as The Godfather or the "Boss of Bosses", Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.

At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.

The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.

He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.

At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.

At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.

In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena.

Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.

His murder sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.

In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was granted house arrest in 2022 but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer. He died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.

In the 1980s, Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.

From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.

In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.

Félix Gallardo's life has been portrayed in a number of television programmes including the Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. The show depicted his rise to power as well as his relationship with Guzmán.

items.title: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
items.summary: The MP lost both of her legs after the alleged attack outside her electorate office four weeks ago.
items.content:
Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.

The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.

In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.

"This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said.

"I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."

She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.

Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.

Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.

Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.

The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.

Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family.

"All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement.

"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation."

'Targeted' attack on much-loved MP leaves Australian town heartbroken

items.title: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker
items.summary: Article URL: https://iter.ca/post/ubo-uxss/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50513160 Points: 545 # Comments: 157
items.content:
Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details.

GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC.

uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page.

The element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html . That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters.

On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation.

On the default setup uBO has a lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, adsbygoogle, war:googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js) filter rule (from uAssets), which hooks fetch . From inside the fetch hook, it makes an XHR request to moz-extension:// /web_accessible_resources/googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js and returns the response from that as the fetch body, instead of actually making the request. The filter rule is intended to replace a network request for JS from an ad server with a dummy script that has the correct API but doesn't do anything.

But the attacker website can itself hook the XHR made from inside the no-fetch-if hook to extract the random extension UUID.

Then the attacker website can run fetch('/adsbygoogle.js').catch(() => {}); to trigger the filter, and make their hooked XHR run. Note that there are several ways that the extension internal UUID could be leaked; it's not just this one filter rule.

Then you can use that to iframe the element picker. Given an iframe element in the page, you just set its src to `moz-extension://${origin}/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html` .

Now we can drive the element picker. We can create a MessageChannel and do iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ what: 'epickerStart' }, '*', [ch.port2]); to send it to the picker iframe. Then we talk to it: it sends us a start message, we send it a showDialog message with a filter and a resultsetDetails message 1 to enable the create button and set opt .

Normally the picker restricts what filters you can enter, and doesn't let you add scriptlet filters. But there's a trick we can do to add arbitrary filters. There's an opt field we set in the second message which is normally the type of network request to match (like image ), and gets appended to the filter with a $ if set, like $image . But since we control it, we can put a newline in it and make it "image\ngoogle.com##+js(trusted-rpnt, script, ...)" to inject an arbitrary trusted filter that injects a script. 2

This is where the main issue is - the element picker shouldn't accept messages from the attacker. One of the fixes was having a secret password that the real element picker gets from the content script, that the element picker sends in the initial postMessage.

I didn't bother actually implementing this, but malicious websites could overlay stuff on top of the embedded element picker or make it invisible by setting the iframe opacity to 0. So as long as the website can get the user to click on the page, it can add arbitrary trusted filters for arbitrary domains.

Filters added by the element picker are always treated as trusted (at least until a recompile), which is why it can add a trusted filter. If the user later changes their custom filters it would cause a recompile, clearing the filter trust. But in practice the attacker could just immediately open the victim webpage, so this doesn't help much.

Originally I sent that message in reply to a dialogSetFilter message from the picker, but it turns out you can just send it right away instead of waiting to reply. ↩︎

items.title: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
items.summary: Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month.
items.content:
Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.

Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend.

The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP.

Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis.

On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in.

A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out.

He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest".

Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close

The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara.

Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time.

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories.

"BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said.

"Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law."

But critics say workers are being sacrificed for factories to churn out products at competitive prices.

Joly Talukder, the vice president of the Garment Workers Trade Union Centre, told BBC's Newshour that "workers have carried the costs for years" while factory owners and global retailers profit from their exploitation.

"They are asking for a wage they can survive on. How can any person of conscience stand against such a basic human demand?" she said.

On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers.

The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November.

Once it is put in place, the revised pay structure is expected to take effect from 1 December.

items.title: Tor Project Issues Rapid-Response DoS-Defense Fix Amid Sustained DDoS Attack
items.summary: Article URL: https://forum.torproject.org/t/security-release-0-4-9-17/22454 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50512441 Points: 221 # Comments: 56
items.content:
Below are the major changes of the released versions and links to more detailed release notes.

Today, we are releasing 0.4.9.17 , which includes a series of security fixes. One fix in particular is especially important for relay DoS defenses related to IPv6 handling.

This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators. This is not an easy problem to address, as relays across the network are being overwhelmed by a massive flood of client circuits. We are actively evaluating additional defenses and so expect further releases in the near future.

We want to extend a huge thank you to all relay operators who have been helping us deal with this ongoing attack. The tor-relays@ mailing list has been very active and we are very grateful for your time, effort, and support. Please, continue doing so!

If you run a relay, please upgrade as soon as possible. No action item is required after upgrading.

My relay is run from tor.exe in my tor browser, how to update it properly?

items.title: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
items.summary: Some Russian tycoons are pining after a return to a 1990s system of oligarchy, when businessmen enjoyed power
items.content:
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.

More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.

Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.

"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."

In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.

That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.

And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.

But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.

The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.

The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule". They had money, which back then meant power.

This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.

But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.

Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.

"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.

Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn).

But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.

Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.

"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round."

And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.

"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic.

And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.

There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health."

If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.

In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios.

Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst.

Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources.

And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests.

This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people.

Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence.

Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take".

He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says.

Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name.

Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians.

But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says.

items.title: Town rebuilt after devastating floods becomes showcase for Libyan strongman's rule
items.summary: The remarkable reconstruction of Derna is being used as a showcase for the rest of Libya by Khalifa Haftar and his sons.
items.content:
"It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna.

Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him.

Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya.

It is part of a rapid $2bn (£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.

The money comes from the state coffers of the oil-rich country, allocated by its parliament. But there are no published records of how it has been spent, raising questions about accountability and possible corruption.

Damdoum, like many flood survivors, simply thanks the head of the Development and Reconstruction Fund, Belkacem Haftar, for what has been achieved since the early hours of 11 September 2023, when lashing rain from Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna, sending a wall of water 7m (23 ft) high cascading down onto the sleeping city.

The exact death toll will probably never be known. Some estimates have been as high as 6,000, though 4,000 now seems a more likely figure. Many bodies are still unidentified.

In a city of about 100,000 people, that means almost everybody lost someone they loved. The 14 relatives and neighbours on the roof with Damdoum – including his father, brother and sister - all drowned.

He survived, but his home was destroyed, and he had to find temporary accommodation. "It was rent, rent, rent," he says. "Now, no-one can take this [new flat] from me. I thank Engineer Belkacem. God sent this person who picked the city up from disaster."

Portraits of Belkacem, widely known simply as "the Engineer", his younger brother Saddam, a military chief also involved in reconstruction, and their father Khalifa are on hoardings all over Derna and the region.

"Since 2011, Libya has not built big projects like this," says Hussein el-Mansory, project manager of the "2,000 Apartments" complex where Damdoum now lives. "I feel very happy and proud and I'll tell my children: 'I made this.'"

The complex includes a new mosque, hospital, shopping mall and schools. New roads, bridges have also been built in Derna. But while many survivors have been rehoused, some are still waiting.

Among them is Izz al-Nasr Ibzeou, a marine science lecturer at the university. His wife Salima, her mother Mouna, and all the couple's seven children, aged between one and 11, drowned.

His family home was ruined, but the authorities have not yet fully restored it because Ibzeou also has an undamaged apartment in another part of town.

He returns every day to his old house, now an empty shell, to see his children's possessions, which he has kept in dust-covered piles.

"This is my son Moez's bike. He played with it every day. And this is my daughter Fawzia's dress. She wore it whenever she went to a wedding," Ibzeou says. "Even if I decide not to come to remember them, my feet will bring me here of their own accord."

To this day, he has not found their bodies. In Derna's vast new flood cemetery, most graves are marked only by numbers, not names, because the process of matching survivors' DNA with corpses is still not completed.

"I go to the cemetery and try to guess where my family are," he says. "This has burned my heart too much. Thank God, I'm patient, but I'm still waiting just to read the Qur'an [at their graves] and say hello to them."

Belkacem Haftar has now extended the work of his reconstruction fund to Libya's second city, Benghazi, and other parts of Libya his father controls.

Libya's parliament, based in the east, last year allocated him a further sum of nearly $11bn, to be spent over three years, in addition to the $2bn it had already given him specifically for Derna.

Building in Benghazi has included new skyscrapers, hospitals, housing developments and a refurbished football stadium that last year hosted a friendly between Inter Milan and Atlético Madrid. Officials have talked in the past about turning the city into a version of "Dubai on the Mediterranean."

Tim Whewell reports on how Derna, famous for its fragrant jasmine flowers, has been rebuilt

If you're in the UK, you can watch Tim's film on Global Eye on BBC 2 on Monday at 19:00.

Outside the UK, you can watch on the BBC World Service YouTube channel , external from Tuesday.

Belkacem tells the BBC he has accomplished more than any previous Libyan administration.

"Libya went through the Gaddafi era, 40 years of neglect and poverty," he said. "The interim governments [post-Gaddafi, based in Tripoli] wasted a lot of money without providing anything the people could touch. I have never made promises to the people. But I have provided them with what they need."

International human rights organisations have repeatedly accused the authorities in eastern Libya and Libyan Arab Armed Forces headed by Khalifa Haftar of serious abuses, including secret executions, arbitrary detentions and forced disappearances.

The Haftars and the Benghazi-based government deny the allegations. Belkacem told the BBC there was complete freedom of speech in eastern Libya.

Critics also say the Haftars have a top-down approach to development, with little public participation in planning decisions, and no transparency.

"There is absolutely zero accountability. We've never seen any financial statements of the Reconstruction Fund, for even the legal on-the-table disbursements of funds," says Claudia Gazzini from the International Crisis Group (ICG) think-tank.

Belkacem says the fund is independently audited and that all contracts are drawn up to high international standards. Dismissing concerns about transparency, he says: "What we've done in Derna was almost impossible. What we care about is the reality, what we do on the ground."

He agreed to show the BBC the audits. But he has not provided them, despite repeated requests.

Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya expert affiliated to the Royal United Services Institute think-tank in London, who has talked to some of the foreign partners awarded construction contracts. He says they are usually obliged to work alongside a private Libyan company linked indirectly to the Haftar family or other powerful political figures.

He says: "What those foreign companies say off the record, is that they do the overwhelming majority of the work and the Libyan partner is often almost an empty shell, in a context where the money is split very often on a 50-50 basis, which indicates that a lot of those facilities and bridges and towers are overcharged, twice as expensive.

"It's a form of overpricing within a context that is utterly opaque, and this is not some fairy coming from the sky that funds these reconstruction efforts. Everything is funded using the public wealth of Libya."

Belkacem Haftar denies the suggestion of corruption in reconstruction projects.

He has said the reconstruction funding was processed through the Central Bank of Libya, which operates on behalf of both the UN-recognised government in the capital Tripoli, in the west of the country, and the government in the eastern city of Benghazi.

"The Haftar authorities used Derna as a showcase for what they were pitching to the rest of Libya," says Gazzini from the ICG.

International efforts to reunite the country have included a proposal by Donald Trump's envoy, Massad Boulos, for a power-sharing deal with Saddam Haftar as Libya's president.

In Derna, there is no plan to rebuild the broken dams, so another disaster on the same scale is unlikely. But there is still a possibility of future flooding.

Gazzini says the authorities failed to take up offers of advice from international experts on ways to reduce the risk, for example by creating flood plains along the river which flows through the town.

"I would have expected a holistic project about how you manage the water flow," Gazzini says.

"But that did not happen. The Libyan side responded more to people's needs, was more interested in having a quick solution to the destruction of the city."

items.title: What's Next for Nvidia?
items.summary: Article URL: https://steveblank.com/2026/11/15/whats-next-for-nvidia/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50512235 Points: 405 # Comments: 512
items.content:
Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned 33 years after he co-founded the company.

What happens to a company when a visionary CEO is gone? Most often innovation dies and the company coasts for years on momentum and its brand. Rarely does it regain its former glory.

That’s the danger facing Nvidia. Here’s what their board should be considering.

Jensen Huang reinvented Nvidia three times. In 2006 he launched CUDA , turning a graphics chip for PC gamers into a general-purpose computing platform – and funded it for years ahead of any revenue. In 2012, when researchers used Nvidia chips to win the ImageNet contest , he pointed the company to deep learning. In 2020, with the acquisition of Mellanox , Nvidia went from selling boards with GPUs to selling integrated racks that power AI datacenters.

These were not just product transitions, but radical business model transitions; new channels, new customers and new markets. Nvidia pivoted from a vendor of graphics boards, to a software platform, and then to systems company. It’s hard to imagine a CEO focused on executing an existing business model funding CUDA through those years.

Steve Jobs did the same at Apple, transforming it from a niche computer company into the most profitable company in the world. Between 2001 and 2008, Jobs reinvented the company three times.

Visionary CEOs are not “just” great at assuring world-class execution of a successful business model, they are also world-class innovators .

The best are agile and know how to pivot, making substantive changes to their business model while or before their market has shifted. The very best of them shape markets – they know how to create new markets by seeing opportunities before anyone else . They remain entrepreneurs .

Visionary CEOs don’t need someone else to demo the company’s key products for them. They deeply understand products, and they have their own coherent and consistent vision of where the industry/business models and customers are today, and where they need to take the company. They know who their customers are because they spend time talking to them. They use strategy committees and the exec staff for advice, but none of these CEOs pivot by committee .

Microsoft and Apple are two examples of what happens when a visionary CEO is replaced by an execution CEO.

Microsoft and the Cost of Missing the Next Market Microsoft entered the 21st century as the dominant software provider for anyone who interacted with a computing device. After running Microsoft for 25 years, Bill Gates handed the reins of Microsoft to Steve Ballmer in January 2000. Ballmer went on to run Microsoft for the next 14 years.

Ballmer organized the company around execution of its then current strengths – Windows and Office businesses. He tripled Microsoft’s sales to $78 billion and profits more than doubled from $9 billion to $22 billion, but those results hid missed opportunities that would reshape computing.

Ballmer failed to understand and execute on the five most important technology trends of the 21st century: in search – losing to Google; in smartphones – losing to Apple; in mobile operating systems – losing to Google/Apple; in media – losing to Apple/Netflix; and in the cloud – losing to Amazon.

In early 2014, Satya Nadella took charge. Nadella got Microsoft organized around the cloud (Azure), freed the Office and Azure teams from Windows and killed the phone business. Nadella saved Microsoft from irrelevance. Today Microsoft is worth about $4 trillion . It is one of the few companies that regained its former glory, after its board replaced a salesman with a product and engineering insider.

Innovation CEOs Hire Execution VPs Successful visionary CEOs build an executive staff of world-class operating executives and technical leaders (and they unconsciously force out any world-class innovators from their direct reports). The problem is in a company driven by a visionary CEO; there is only one visionary.

Nvidia is the extreme case. Jensen had about 60 direct reports and discouraged one-on-one meetings. No long-term plans. Much like Jobs, he made himself the point where technical, product and business decisions came together. Replacing that role is harder than filling a box on an organization chart. He said he didn’t believe in succession planning .

When visionary founders depart (resignation, death, firing, etc.), their operating executives believe it’s their turn to run the company. At Microsoft, Bill Gates chose Steve Ballmer, and at Apple Steve Jobs chose Tim Cook. Jensen anointed no one.

Once in charge, one of the first things these operations/execution CEOs do is to get rid of the chaos and turbulence in the organization. Execution CEOs value stability, process and repeatable execution. On one hand that’s great for predictability, but it often starts a creative death spiral – creative people start to leave, and other executors (without the innovation talent of the old leader) are put into more senior roles – hiring more process people, which in turn forces out the remaining creative talent. This culture shift ripples down from the top and what once felt like a company on a mission to change the world now feels like another job .

(Amazon is a counterexample. Before succeeding Jeff Bezos, Andy Jassy had already founded and led AWS . He was an innovator who had built a new business inside the existing company.)

At Nvidia this step isn’t optional. No one else can run a company with 60 direct reports, so the next CEO’s first move will be to add layers of management.

Why Tim Cook Was the New Steve Ballmer Tim Cook ran Apple for 15 years. Apple under Cook grew its revenues from $108 billion to $416 billion and its market value from $350 billion to about $4 trillion. The iPhone continued its annual upgrades of incremental improvements. The transition to Apple silicon showed that major technical change on the chip level was possible under his leadership. But Apple silicon was a better engine for the existing products Apple already had, not a new market.

Apple stumbled badly on the one major product category launched under Cook – Apple Vision Pro and missed badly on AI (Siri was actually first with a Chatbot.) This year it turned to Google to help fix Siri. In September 2026 Cook handed the job to John Ternus.

How Nvidia Could Miss the Boat The threat to Nvidia is already visible: its biggest customers are becoming its competitors. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Tesla are all building their own AI chips . Jensen’s answer was to keep innovating and bring to market a new generation of chips every year, build a moat around an integrated hardware and software platform ( CUDA ), and invest ~$50 billion in the AI labs that run on Nvidia.

It’s likely these are the bets an execution CEO trims first.

The irony is that in the 21st century, the tighter you hold on to your current product/markets, the likelier you will be disrupted . The rapid change of technology will create new disruptions that will force “bet the company” decisions about product direction, markets, pricing, supply chain, operations and the reorganization necessary to execute a new business model. In the GPU market, the difference between market dominance and Chapter 11 may be a hands-on product/customer, and business model-centric CEO with an entrepreneurial vision of the future.

Four Challenges for the Board of Directors The dilemma facing the board at Nvidia or any board of directors on the departure of an innovative CEO is strategic : Do we still want to be an innovative, risk taking company? Or should we now focus on execution of our core business, reduce our risky bets and maximize shareholder return. Ultimately a board would like both – preserving the speed and ambition of Jensen’s decision-making while distributing enough authority for the company to function without him.

Tactically , that question results in asking: Do you search for another innovator from outside, promote one of the executors or go deeper down the organization to find an innovator?

“The cemeteries of the worrld are filled with indispensable men.”

There is no question that Jensen Huang is a brilliant innovator, visionary, and company builder, but he is also a man filled to overflowing with hubris and a reckless disregard for his fiduciary duty to his shareholders.

He held views as to Chinese use of Nvidia’s bleeding edge chips with which reasonable men can disagree with equally sound logic.

While all that you say in regard to Apple/Jobs and MS/Gates is true, the performance of both of those companies post founder departure was and is superb. If those exemplars define the downside, I will load up on Nvidia before their earnings call on Tuesday.

The Board should be horsewhipped for having allowed Huang to violate what are sound and reasonable business principles as to span of control and continuity. The Board — taking no issue with the man’s brilliance as an innovator — should have insisted that there be a foundation for the eventuality that has, in fact, presented itself.

items.title: Google spegne il motore di ricerca alle scuole che rifiutano l’ia
items.summary: Negli Stati Uniti chi vuole tenere l’intelligenza artificiale fuori dalle aule dovrà rinunciare anche al motore di ricerca. La scelta ha scatenato le proteste di genitori, insegnanti e politici Leggi
items.content:
Il 3 novembre Google ha annunciato che dall’inizio del 2027 i suoi strumenti di intelligenza artificiale saranno disattivati per gli studenti delle scuole statunitensi, da quella dell’infanzia alle superiori, a meno che i dirigenti scolastici non decidano di attivarli. Sembra una concessione a chi chiede più controllo sul rapporto tra bambini e chatbot.

Ma c’è un problema, spiega il New York Times: le scuole che rifiuteranno del tutto l’ia perderanno anche l’accesso a Google Search, il motore di ricerca dell’azienda. “La ricerca e l’ia sono profondamente integrate”, ha detto Chris Phillips, vicepresidente di Google per l’istruzione. Nelle scuole che hanno vietato l’ia, ha aggiunto, gli studenti non avranno accesso al motore di ricerca e vedranno un messaggio d’avviso che il servizio non è disponibile.

La decisione pesa particolarmente perché Google è ovunque nelle scuole statunitensi. I Chromebook, i computer portatili economici dell’azienda, sono i dispositivi più distribuiti agli studenti. Sull’Atlantic il giornalista Will Oremus li descrive come un “cavallo di Troia” dell’intelligenza artificiale nelle scuole.

Con un Chromebook scolastico basta aprire l’app Gemini per farsi scrivere un tema. Oppure si può digitare un problema di algebra nella barra di ricerca e ottenere la soluzione già pronta in un Ai Overview, il riassunto generato automaticamente dall’intelligenza artificiale in cima ai risultati.

Negli ultimi mesi la resistenza di genitori e insegnanti è cresciuta. A settembre i due distretti scolastici più grandi del paese, New York e Los Angeles, hanno limitato l’accesso degli studenti all’ia generativa sui dispositivi a scuola. La settimana prima dell’annuncio di Google, lo stato di New York ha approvato una legge sulla sicurezza dei chatbot che vieta alle aziende di offrire ai minori diverse funzioni dell’intelligenza artificiale.

Il sindaco di New York Zohran Mamdani ha scritto sui social media : “Nessuna azienda dovrebbe avere il potere di imporci come educare i nostri figli”. Lina Khan, ex presidente della Federal trade commission, l’autorità statunitense per la concorrenza, ha accusato Google di usare il suo “monopolio della ricerca sul web per costringere le scuole” ad adottare la sua intelligenza artificiale, Gemini.

Ad agosto Google aveva attivato per impostazione predefinita le funzioni di ia dentro Classroom, la piattaforma usata per assegnare i compiti. La novità valeva per gli studenti di tutte le età, nelle scuole che già consentivano l’accesso a Gemini. Alcuni dirigenti avevano protestato.

“Un distretto scolastico non dovrebbe adottare per sbaglio una piattaforma di ia solo perché sei mesi fa nessuno ha trovato la casella giusta da spuntare per la rinuncia”, aveva detto James O’Hagan, responsabile dell’innovazione di un distretto del Wisconsin. “La regola dovrebbe essere la scelta, non l’adozione automatica”. Ora Google ha fatto marcia indietro su quel meccanismo, ma sulla ricerca non cede.

L’azienda sostiene che le critiche nascano da un equivoco. “Gli annunci di oggi danno alle scuole più scelta, non meno”, ha scritto su X. È vero, osserva l’Atlantic: Google non ha mai offerto una versione della ricerca senza ia (c’è solo una scheda “Web” che mostra unicamente i link), e ora sia Gemini sia Search saranno spenti per impostazione predefinita, con la possibilità di attivarli.

Per le scuole che sceglieranno di riattivare il motore di ricerca ci saranno due opzioni. La prima include gli Ai Overviews e le chat con l’ia, come la versione per il pubblico. La seconda si basa su Guided learning, una funzione di Gemini che dovrebbe guidare lo studente passo dopo passo senza dargli le risposte.

Ma in un test del New York Times la versione per il pubblico di Guided learning ha prodotto un tema dettagliato su una traccia di storia. La versione scolastica, ancora in fase di sperimentazione, avrà più limiti: per esempio, gli insegnanti potranno leggere le conversazioni degli studenti con il chatbot.

Resta il fatto che Google non offre quello che le scuole chiedono di più: una ricerca tradizionale, senza risposte generate. Come vorrebbe il distretto di Los Angeles. Lo chiede anche Richard Culatta, amministratore delegato di Iste+Ascd, un’organizzazione non profit che promuove l’uso della tecnologia nelle scuole e che pure ha ricevuto finanziamenti da Google.

La logica dell’azienda, spiega l’Atlantic, è che in un certo senso tutta la ricerca è già basata sull’intelligenza artificiale: da anni Google usa modelli linguistici per ordinare i risultati. Ma genitori e insegnanti non contestano l’algoritmo che decide quali link mostrare. Contestano un motore di ricerca trasformato in una macchina che dà risposte istantanee, soggette a errori, e che abitua i ragazzi a delegare il pensiero critico e alla valutazione delle fonti.

Dietro la linea di Google c’è anche una ragione commerciale. I chatbot sono la minaccia più seria mai affrontata dal motore di ricerca: la OpenAiI sostiene che ChatGptPT gestisce ormai un volume di ricerche pari a circa un quinto di quello di Google. E, secondo l’Atlantic, Google scommette che la comodità vincerà sui dubbi.

Intanto qualcuno cerca alternative: DuckDuckGo , un motore di ricerca attento alla privacy degli utenti, afferma che l’uso della sua opzione di ricerca senza ia è cresciuto del 30 per cento da settembre, e che sta studiando un modo per aiutare le scuole che rinunceranno a Google a cambiare il motore di ricerca predefinito.

Kelly Clancy, madre di un ragazzo che frequenta la seconda media in una scuola pubblica di New York, è alla guida di alcuni gruppi che chiedono una moratoria sull’ia nelle scuole. Racconta che il figlio usa Google ogni giorno per i compiti, come una recente ricerca di scienze sulla sicurezza in laboratorio. “Dobbiamo ripensare da zero il modo in cui insegniamo ai ragazzi a fare ricerca”, dice. Magari, suggerisce, tornando in biblioteca, o usando altri motori di ricerca che permettono di controllare meglio l’ia.

Secondo Morgan Polikoff, che insegna scienze dell’educazione alla University of Southern California, la scelta di Google potrebbe dare nuova forza al movimento di genitori e insegnanti contro la tecnologia a scuola: “È un esempio particolarmente chiaro di come l’industria tecnologica faccia di tutto per imporci l’ia, anche quando abbiamo detto che non la vogliamo”. ◆

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, le news. Pechino: “Pace mondiale al centro del vertice Xi-Trump-Putin”
items.summary: Zelensky: “Distrutto il 55% della capacità di raffinazione del petrolio russo”. Lavrov ribadisce le condizioni fissate da Putin nel 2024: ritiro ucraino da quattro regioni e rinuncia all’Alleanza atlantica. Kiev colpisce il Ponte di Crimea: traffico sospeso
items.content:
La Russia ribadisce le sue condizioni per mettere fine alla guerra in Ucraina e respinge l'ipotesi di un ingresso di Kiev nella Nato . Il ministro degli Esteri Sergei Lavrov conferma che gli obiettivi fissati da Vladimir Putin nel giugno 2024 restano invariati: il ritiro delle truppe ucraine dalle quattro regioni rivendicate da Mosca e la rinuncia all'adesione all'Alleanza atlantica. Una posizione che allontana le prospettive di un'intesa con Washington . Intanto, il Cremlino torna ad alzare i toni nei confronti dell'Europa , avvertendo che, in assenza di un accordo su una nuova architettura di sicurezza continentale, la Russia potrebbe ricorrere alla forza. Nella notte più di cento droni diretti verso Mosca sono stati intercettati dalla Russia.

Cremlino: “Incontro Putin e Xi prima del trilaterale, anche sull'Ucraina”

Nuove sanzioni Ue, nel mirino disinformazione russa e gruppo di hacker

Commissione Ue: “Pronti a ospitare colloqui multilaterali, anche con Russia”

Cremlino contro Zelensky: “Non si svelano i dettagli dei negoziati”

Fonti Usa: “Al trilaterale vertice con Putin e Xi Trump vuole evitare di parlare della guerra in Ucraina”

La Russia ha intercettato oltre 100 droni diretti verso Mosca durante la notte

Pechino conferma trilaterale Xi, Trump e Putin: il 19 dicembre a Shenzhen

Lavrov: “Gli alleati di Mosca sono l'esercito, la marina, l'aeronautica e il nucleare”

Gli alleati della Russia sono l'esercito, la marina, le forze aerospaziali e le forze nucleari, ha dichiarato il ministro degli Esteri russo, Serghei Lavrov in un'intervista alla Tv di Stato. "Il nostro mondo non si sta semplificando. Ricordate: abbiamo due alleati, l'esercito e la marina, e ora abbiamo anche le forze aerospaziali e, naturalmente, le forze nucleari", ha affermato il ministro russo, citato da Tass. (

Nei colloqui con gli Stati Uniti non bisogna parlare "a bocca aperta per l'ammirazione", pena la mancata tutela dei propri interessi, ha affermato il ministrro degli Esteri russo, Serghei Lavrov, in un'intervista per la Tv di Stato. "Dire che Washington ha fatto un passo audace revocando le sanzioni sulle forniture di diesel russo è un errore", ha affermato il ministro russo, citato da Tass. "Le sanzioni non sono state revocate, sono ancora in vigore, avevano solo bisogno di calmare il mercato per un paio di giornì", ha chiarito Lavrov. "Dobbiamo essere realisti, dobbiamo parlare con gli americani, ma quando si cerca di farlo con aria di giubilo, non si tutelano i propri interessi e gli americani non rispettano questo tipo di comportamento", ha sottolineato il ministro. I colloqui russo-americani sulla rimozione dei punti di attrito stanno procedendo "così-così", ha dichiarato il ministro degli Esteri nella stessa intervista. "Procedono lentamente, nonostante ogni volta che incontro (il segretario di Stato Usa) Rubio - ci siamo incontrati a New York e poi ad Atlanta al G20 - glielo ricordi".

Lavrov: “L’Europa ha avuto molte opportunità di mediare sulla questione ucraina”

"L'Europa ha avuto diverse opportunità di mediare sulla questione ucraina", ha dichiarato il ministro degli Esteri russo, Serghei Lavrov, in un'intervista per la Tv di stato russa. "L'Europa ha avuto diverse opportunità di svolgere un ruolo di mediazione, a partire dal febbraio 2014, quando Francia, Germania e Polonia hanno agito come garanti dell'accordo tra Yanukovych (l'ex presidente ucraino) e l'opposizione", ha osservato Lavrov, citato da Tass. "Sappiamo tutti come è andata a finire", ha concluso il ministro degli Esteri russo

Nei colloqui sul futuro dell'Ucraina "penso che ci sia lavoro per tutti gli esperti che abbiamo nel Seae. Spero che non si creino strutture parallele che pesino sul bilancio" dell'Ue. Lo sottolinea l'Alta Rappresentante dell'Ue Kaja Kallas, in conferenza stampa a Bruxelles. Nel Seae, il servizio diplomatico dell'Ue, "abbiamo persone esperte e penso che debbano essere usate", conclude.

Cremlino: “Trilaterale Putin-Xi-Trump previsto il 19 novembre alle 19.30 italiane”

Un incontro tra il presidente russo Vladimir Putin, il presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump e il presidente cinese Xi Jinping a margine del il vertice Apec di Shenzhen è previsto per le 14:30 ora locale (7:30 italiane) di giovedì presso la Residenza Presidenziale Cinese, ha annunciato il consigliere presidenziale russo, Yuri Ushakov. "Probabilmente l'evento più interessante è previsto per le 14:30: l'incontro trilaterale tra Vladimir Putin, il presidente cinese Xi Jinping e il presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump".

I leader di Russia e Stati Uniti, Vladimir Putin e Donald Trump, si incontreranno di certo al vertice Apec a Shenzhen, ma in che formato e dove è da decidere. Lo ha confermato il consigliere di Putin Yuri Ushakov. "Posso dire al 100% che, dato che Putin e Donald Trump saranno insieme a Shenzhen, ovviamente si incontreranno lì", ha spiegato durante un briefing, ma si sta ancora concordando la natura di questo incontro e dove si terrà esattamente.

Cremlino: “Incontro Putin e Xi prima del trilaterale, anche sull'Ucraina”

Putin e Xi Jinping terranno colloqui il 18 novembre ha annunciato il consigliere presidenziale russo Yurij Ushakov. L'incontro si svolgerà durante una colazione di lavoro e si concentrerà su questioni di politica estera, tra cui la situazione in Ucraina. "Si parla di un formato molto ristretto. Le parti discuteranno della cooperazione strategica nella regione Asia-Pacifico, naturalmente, dell'Ucraina, della penisola coreana e così via", ha detto Ushakov citato da Interfax.

Una giovane donna russa è stata arrestata dall'Fsb in merito all'attentato dinamitardo contro Sergei Zavorotny, consigliere e portavoce dell'ex primo ministro ucraino Mykola Azarov. Lo rende noto l'agenzia di stampa Ria Novosti. Una bomba, collocata nell'auto di Zavorotny, è esplosa a Mosca lo scorso 13 novembre, ferendolo in modo grave. Le autorità stanno indagando per tentato omicidio e Zavorotny resta ricoverato in ospedale. "Il Servizio di sicurezza federale, in collaborazione con il ministero degli Interni, ha arrestato a Mosca una cittadina russa, nata nel 2005. La donna è coinvolta nell'attentato dinamitardo contro l'auto di una personalità pubblica e giornalista indipendente, su ordine dei servizi segreti ucraini", si legge nel comunicato. Secondo i servizi di intelligence, la giovane donna è stata "adescata" da truffatori e ha trasferito una grossa somma di denaro su un "conto sicuro" presso la Banca Centrale Russa, che i criminali hanno utilizzato per esercitare ulteriori pressioni su di lei.

Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha ringraziato la Commissione europea e il Consiglio Ue per aver approvato "il più grande pagamento unico mai effettuato" a favore dell'Ucraina nell'ambito dello Strumento per l'Ucraina (Ukraine Facility), pari a quasi 8 miliardi di euro. In un messaggio sui social, il leader ucraino ha rivolto un ringraziamento particolare alla presidente della Commissione, Ursula von der Leyen, per aver accelerato l'erogazione dei fondi, sottolineando le crescenti necessità di bilancio del Paese in vista dell'inverno e dei "più intensi attacchi russi" contro reti energetiche, sistemi di riscaldamento, approvvigionamento idrico e altre infrastrutture critiche. Zelensky ha evidenziato che il via libera al pagamento segue l'attuazione da parte di Kiev di oltre 20 impegni di riforma concordati con l'Unione europea e dimostra che l'Ucraina "mantiene quanto concordato con l'Ue". Per questo, ha aggiunto, i progressi compiuti dovrebbero riflettersi anche nell'apertura dei due cluster negoziali ancora mancanti nel percorso di adesione all'Unione. "La resilienza finanziaria dell'Ucraina è fondamentale per garantire la nostra sicurezza europea condivisa", ha concluso.

La Commissaria per i diritti umani della Federazione Russa, Yana Lantratova, ha detto ai giornalisti che lo scampio di prigionieri tra la Russia e l'Ucraina, annunciato nell'ambito dei negoziati trilaterali ad Abu Dhabi, "è in preparazione". Ne dà notizia la Tass. "Stiamo preparando un ampio scambio, come già annunciato. Si tratta di questioni molto delicate", ha detto Lantratova.

Kiev: “Importante l'Ue al tavolo dei negoziati, da Mosca nessun segnale di pace”

"È davvero importante, ed è del tutto opportuno, che i nostri partner europei siedano al tavolo delle trattative; tuttavia, mi sembra che i russi non abbiano dato alcun segnale concreto o tangibile della loro disponibilità ad abbandonare questa guerra. Il nostro obiettivo è ottenere un cessate il fuoco. Vogliamo raggiungere una pace giusta e duratura, ma non una resa". Lo ha detto il premier ucraino Sergii Koretskyi intervenendo al Forum sull'allargamento Ue 2026. "Cogliamo ogni reale opportunità per porre fine a questo conflitto, non attraverso una resa, ma fermando le ostilità, ottenendo un cessate il fuoco e giungendo a una pace giusta e duratura", ha aggiunto. Quanto all'adesione all'Ue, "non ci troviamo in una situazione ordinaria, né in un momento consueto per l'Ucraina. Per questo - ha spiegato - vorremmo individuare, insieme agli Stati membri dell'Ue e alla Commissione, una soluzione non convenzionale, valutando ogni possibile passo che possa favorire l'ingresso dell'Ucraina nell'Unione europea. Da parte nostra, faremo tutto ciò che è in nostro potere per raggiungere questo obiettivo".
